main.title: Homefront
main.subtitle: War enters familiar streets
main.summary: Homefront places its resistance fighters in a fictional occupied United States. Familiar streets, civilian spaces and military spectacle frame a shooter built around the uneasy distance between home and battlefield.

cards.heading: Familiar places under occupation
cards.text: Kaos Studios sets Homefront in familiar American streets transformed by occupation. Residential neighbourhoods, schools, petrol stations and sports fields show traces of their earlier use alongside military control and shortages. Creative director David Votypka described the approach as taking familiar places and making them alien.

cards.heading: Battle Points as a tactical currency
cards.text: Multiplayer awards Battle Points for kills, assists and objectives during a match. Players can spend them on equipment, support actions or vehicles rather than waiting for permanent unlocks. Saving for a more expensive option competes with buying something immediately useful. Vehicles are purchased at respawn, linking their arrival to that decision.

cards.heading: A fictional history before the first mission
cards.text: The story imagines an occupied United States in 2027. THQ credited John Milius with helping shape it and consulted a former CIA agent on the fictional sequence of events. The resulting background gives context to the propaganda, resistance and civilian spaces encountered during the campaign.

main.title: MotorStorm: Apocalypse
main.subtitle: A race through a city coming apart
main.summary: MotorStorm: Apocalypse is Evolution Studios' PlayStation 3 racing game, first released in Australia on 17 March 2011. The festival moves into an abandoned city damaged by a natural disaster, where the route can change while the competitors are still using it. Buildings collapse, surfaces break and streets become unstable parts of the race. Three riders provide perspectives on the event across different difficulty levels. The setting replaces Pacific Rift's island with an urban course whose destruction is planned into the timing of the competition.

cards.heading: A race through a city coming apart
cards.text: MotorStorm: Apocalypse is Evolution Studios' PlayStation 3 racing game, first released in Australia on 17 March 2011. The festival moves into an abandoned city damaged by a natural disaster, where the route can change while the competitors are still using it. Buildings collapse, surfaces break and streets become unstable parts of the race. Three riders provide perspectives on the event across different difficulty levels. The setting replaces Pacific Rift's island with an urban course whose destruction is planned into the timing of the competition.

cards.heading: The next lap may have a different road
cards.text: A course is not always a fixed arrangement to memorise. A collapse can expose another path or remove the one a racer expected to follow, asking the player to read movement in the scenery as well as the vehicles ahead. Different classes still compete together, carrying different advantages through the city's narrow and open sections. Boost supplies a temporary burst of speed at the risk of overheating. Knowing when to commit matters particularly when the route itself is moving, falling or opening beneath the approaching field.

cards.heading: The festival and the real disaster
cards.text: Apocalypse expanded local play with four-player split-screen and offered online races with sixteen competitors, alongside vehicle customisation and progression features. Its release coincided with the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, leading Sony to postpone launches in several regions. The Australian launch went ahead before further shipments were halted. That timing became a significant part of the release's history, separate from the fictional disaster built into its courses. Its music combined orchestral and electronic contributors, supporting a racing game organised around sudden changes in speed, scenery and available space.

main.title: Crysis 2
main.subtitle: Crytek brings the series to a wider set of platforms
main.summary: Crysis 2 is a first-person shooter video game developed by Crytek, published by Electronic Arts and released in North America, Australia and Europe in March 2011 for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360.

cards.heading: Crytek brings the series to a wider set of platforms
cards.text: Crysis 2 is a first-person shooter video game developed by Crytek, published by Electronic Arts and released in North America, Australia and Europe in March 2011 for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360. Officially announced on June 1, 2009, the game is the second main installment of the Crysis series, and a sequel to the 2007 video game Crysis, and its expansion Crysis Warhead. The story was written by Richard Morgan, while Peter Watts was consulted and wrote a novel adaptation of the game. It was the first game to showcase the CryEngine 3 game engine and the first game using the engine to be released on consoles. A sequel, Crysis 3, was released in 2013. A remastered version, titled Crysis 2 Remastered and following in the steps of Crysis Remastered, was released in 2021 for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One, also bundled as part of the Crysis Remastered Trilogy compilation.

cards.heading: An urban jungle replaces the island
cards.text: Crysis 2 is a first-person shooter. The player assumes the role of a Force Recon Marine called Alcatraz. Similar to its predecessor, it provides freedom to customize weaponry and abilities. Crytek wanted to avoid making another game set in a true jungle environment (as were Far Cry and Crysis); New York City has been dubbed an "urban jungle". The urban atmosphere offers new options with relation to progressing and planning attacks. Players are able to navigate between floors and buildings, as well as a destroyed cityscape.

cards.heading: Nanosuit modes shape the approach
cards.text: The new Nanosuit supports new and upgraded features. Suit functionality has been streamlined; multiple modes can easily be used simultaneously whenever the user wishes. The first suit's Strength and Speed Modes have been combined into the new Power Mode, the suit binoculars function has been upgraded with an advanced Tactical mode, the Cloaking Device has been modified to allow increased sensory input and silent melee stealth kills and has been renamed to Stealth Mode, while the Armor Mode has been left more or less as is, with the exception of slightly restricted agility and an ever-decreasing energy level.

main.title: Patapon 3
main.subtitle: An Uberhero takes the drums onto the battlefield
main.summary: Patapon 3 concentrates the PSP series around an Uberhero, a smaller fighting party and expanded multiplayer. Drum patterns remain the link between the player, the music and the warriors' actions.

cards.heading: A new hero after the tribe turns to stone
cards.text: Patapon 3 arrived on PSP in North America on 12 April 2011, developed by Pyramid and Japan Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment. After the tribe opens a forbidden vessel and is turned to stone, the player's divine presence merges with a fallen warrior to create the Uberhero. The new avatar stands within the battlefield instead of remaining an invisible god directing a large army from outside it.

cards.heading: Classes and equipment shape a smaller party
cards.text: The Uberhero fights alongside a much smaller group, including the warriors Ton, Chin and Kan and the flag-bearing Hatapon. Character classes, equipment and an experience-point system give individual fighters a greater role in progression. The PSP's four face buttons still act as drums: the player must enter rhythmic patterns to issue commands. Developing a party does not replace the beat-matching system; it changes the fighters who respond to it.

cards.heading: Rhythmic orders shared with other players
cards.text: Multiplayer takes a more prominent place than in the previous games. Players can join cooperative adventures or take part in competitive battles, connecting nearby PSP systems or playing over the internet. The Pata-Text system provides a way to communicate with other players. This broader emphasis on shared play accompanies new weapons, classes and missions, while keeping the series' recognizable silhouettes and its connection between music and tactical movement.

main.title: Portal 2
main.subtitle: Back to Aperture Science
main.summary: Portal 2 is a 2011 first person puzzle-platform game developed by Valve for Windows, macOS, Linux, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360.

cards.heading: A return to Aperture Science
cards.text: Portal 2 is a 2011 first person puzzle-platform game developed by Valve for Windows, macOS, Linux, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360. The retail versions and PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions were distributed by Electronic Arts. A port for the Nintendo Switch was released as part of the Portal: Companion Collection in June 2022.

cards.heading: Portals, gels and a cooperative campaign
cards.text: Portal 2 returns to Chell and GLaDOS inside a damaged Aperture Science. Wheatley and recordings of founder Cave Johnson introduce new parts of its history. Excursion Funnels, lasers, light bridges and gels expand the puzzles, changing movement and which surfaces can accept portals. A separate cooperative campaign gives Atlas and P-Body puzzles built for two players. Ellen McLain, Stephen Merchant and J. K. Simmons voice its central characters, with songs by Jonathan Coulton and the National.

cards.heading: Promotion and player-made chambers
cards.text: Valve announced Portal 2 in March 2010, and promoted it with alternate reality games including the Potato Sack, a collaboration with several independent game developers. After release, Valve released downloadable content and a simplified map editor to allow players to create and share levels.

cards.heading: Puzzles, writing and performances
cards.text: Portal 2 received critical acclaim for its gameplay, balanced learning curve, pacing, dark humor, writing, and acting. Like its predecessor, it has been described as one of the greatest video games ever made by numerous publications and critics.

main.title: Mortal Kombat
main.subtitle: A new beginning for Mortal Kombat
main.summary: Mortal Kombat (also known as Mortal Kombat 9 (MK9)) is a 2011 fighting game developed by NetherRealm Studios and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment.

cards.heading: A new beginning for Mortal Kombat
cards.text: Mortal Kombat (also known as Mortal Kombat 9 (MK9)) is a 2011 fighting game developed by NetherRealm Studios and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. It is the ninth main installment in the Mortal Kombat franchise and a soft reboot of the series. The game was released for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 systems in April 2011, and a PlayStation Vita port was released in May 2012. An expanded version of the game, titled Mortal Kombat: Komplete Edition, was released for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 in February 2012 and for Microsoft Windows in July 2013.

cards.heading: A two-dimensional fighting plane
cards.text: Principal gameplay involves one-on-one 2.5D-style fighting. Mortal Kombat uses a single two-dimensional fighting plane (at 60 frames per second), although characters are rendered in three-dimensional fashion, intended to give depth and range to portrayals of various projectiles. Unlike previous Mortal Kombat games, four buttons on the game controller represent attacks and are each linked to a corresponding limb.

cards.heading: The meter connects defence and special attacks
cards.text: A new feature is the "super meter", which can be charged by various actions during battle such as performing special moves, getting blocked by the opponent, or getting hit by them. The super meter can be charged to three levels, each of them enabling a different action to be performed. At the first level, it can be used to deliver an enhanced version of one of the character's special attacks; two levels can be used to interrupt a combo attack, and the full three levels allow for the delivery of a special attack called an "X-ray move". The X-ray move unleashes a series of attacks during which the game provides an internal view of the character being attacked, which shows their bones and organs being broken or ruptured.

main.title: Terraria
main.summary: Terraria is a 2011 action-adventure video game developed and published by Re-Logic.

cards.heading: A world to explore, fight and reshape
cards.text: Terraria is a 2011 action-adventure video game developed and published by Re-Logic. As a sandbox game, Terraria has no set goals. After creating the player character and choosing the game's difficulty, the player is placed in a two-dimensional, procedurally generated world where they explore, fight enemies, gather resources, and craft equipment. Players beat bosses, a tougher variety of enemies, to gain access to more items, resources, and equipment. By completing select goals, players receive access to non-player characters (NPCs) who sell items and offer services, such as healing and fishing quests. Terraria can be played alone or with others, and features support for modding.

cards.heading: A small team and years of updates
cards.text: Andrew Spinks commenced development in January 2011; he was assisted by a team of game testers and designers. As of 2025, Terraria is developed by eleven members of Re-Logic. Initially released in May 2011 on the Steam digital store, Terraria has received continuous content updates that have considerably changed it from its first version. The game was originally set to end development in 2012, but it resumed in 2013.

main.title: The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings
main.subtitle: Geralt between monsters and kings
main.summary: The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a 2011 action role-playing game developed by CD Projekt Red, based on Andrzej Sapkowski's fantasy novels.

cards.heading: Geralt returns
cards.text: The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a 2011 action role-playing game developed by CD Projekt Red, based on The Witcher series of fantasy novels authored by Andrzej Sapkowski. It is a sequel to the 2007 game, The Witcher and the second main installment in The Witcher's video game series. It was released for Windows, Xbox 360, OS X, and Linux.

cards.heading: A wider combat arsenal
cards.text: The gameplay of The Witcher 2 is a marked departure from that of its predecessor. Combat, for instance, is more complex, with additions in the form of abilities to lay traps and aim and throw ranged weapons. The protagonist, Geralt, has an improved offensive and defensive arsenal, with a range of melee and ranged weapons, armor, bombs, traps, and secondary weapons such as hatchets and shovels.

cards.heading: Four paths of development
cards.text: Upgrades are divided into four paths: an initial training path, which includes generalized upgrades for core abilities and must be invested in before the other paths can be accessed; swordsmanship, which improves Geralt's sword-fighting abilities; alchemy, which includes perks such as reducing the negative effects of potions; and magic, which improves Witcher Signs.

cards.heading: A monster hunter in a political struggle
cards.text: Geralt's profession is hunting monsters, but his journey also passes through struggles for power in the Northern Kingdoms. The developer describes a nonlinear story in which decisions can have serious consequences. The adventure contains different story paths and multiple endings, making the player's choices part of how events unfold rather than merely a way to select equipment. Trading settlements, mining towns, castles and fortresses provide the setting for these encounters and conflicts.

main.title: L.A. Noire
main.subtitle: A detective in postwar Los Angeles
main.summary: L.A. Noire is a 2011 action-adventure video game developed by Team Bondi and published by Rockstar Games.

cards.heading: A detective in postwar Los Angeles
cards.text: L.A. Noire is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Team Bondi and published by Rockstar Games. Set in Los Angeles in 1947, the game follows the rise of detective Cole Phelps through the ranks of the Los Angeles Police Department as he solves a range of cases across various bureaus. When he is tasked with investigating a morphine distribution ring involving several of his former squadmates from World War II, Phelps finds both his personal and professional life falling into turmoil, and reluctantly joins forces with his estranged former comrade, Jack Kelso, to uncover a major conspiracy involving prominent Los Angeles figures.

cards.heading: Cases unfold across the city
cards.text: The game is played from a third-person perspective. The player may freely roam its interactive open world, primarily in a vehicle or on foot. As the game progresses, the player advances through several police department bureaus—Patrol, Traffic, Homicide, Vice, and Arson. The story is divided into multiple "cases", during which players must investigate crime scenes for clues, follow up leads, and interrogate suspects and witnesses; the player's success at these activities impacts how much of each case's story is revealed and their overall rating. The game features fast-paced action sequences, including chases, combat, and gunfights. Outside of cases, the player can complete optional street crimes and collect items found around the game world.

cards.heading: Evidence changes the interrogation
cards.text: While solving cases, the player discovers evidence, including information from non-player characters or physical clues found in or around crime scenes, locations of interest, or dead bodies; several pieces of physical evidence can be manipulated or further investigated to discover more information. When all key clues are discovered at a crime scene, the investigation music concludes. The player can also use telephones or gamewells to contact the police radio and access additional information. During cases, the player interrogates suspects and witnesses to discover information. When the interviewee responds, the player is given the option to either believe them, doubt them, or accuse them of lying. If the player accuses them of lying, they must submit evidence to prove it. The player's in-game notebook is used to list evidence, locations, and people involved in the case, as well as to select questions during interrogations.

cards.heading: MotionScan brings performances into the investigation
cards.text: The development of L.A. Noire began following Team Bondi's founding in 2004, and was assisted by multiple Rockstar studios worldwide. L.A. Noire uses the proprietary motion capture technology MotionScan, which captures actors' facial expressions from every angle, resulting in a realistic recreation of a human face essential for the game's interrogations. As part of their research for the open world, the development team conducted field research in Los Angeles. The game features an original score inspired by 1940s films, and contains licensed music of songs from the era. The game was delayed numerous times through its seven-year development, which included a change of publisher and platforms. The working hours and managerial style of the studio was met with public complaints from staff members, and Team Bondi closed shortly after the game's initial release.

main.title: Dead or Alive: Dimensions
main.subtitle: Four tournaments in a portable arena
main.summary: Dead or Alive: Dimensions is Team Ninja's Nintendo 3DS fighting game bringing together the characters and story of the series' first four main instalments. Its Chronicle mode revisits those tournaments through different fighters, while a roster of twenty-six includes previously unplayable bosses. The upper screen carries the action and the touchscreen provides access to move information. The compilation gives a new audience a route through an established cast. It also brings the series' close-range exchanges and hazardous arenas to a Nintendo system for the first time.

cards.heading: Four tournaments in a portable arena
cards.text: Dead or Alive: Dimensions is Team Ninja's Nintendo 3DS fighting game bringing together the characters and story of the series' first four main instalments. Its Chronicle mode revisits those tournaments through different fighters, while a roster of twenty-six includes previously unplayable bosses. The upper screen carries the action and the touchscreen provides access to move information. The compilation gives a new audience a route through an established cast. It also brings the series' close-range exchanges and hazardous arenas to a Nintendo system for the first time.

cards.heading: Read the attack before answering
cards.text: The series' relationship between strikes, throws and defensive holds gives an opponent's intention practical importance. A successful response depends on recognising what is coming and committing to the appropriate action. Training and the move display help make those options visible on a handheld, while the three-dimensional arenas provide opportunities to force a fighter into a dangerous position. The familiar cast gives returning players recognisable styles to investigate. For a newcomer, choosing one character becomes a way to learn a particular set of answers before approaching the wider roster.

cards.heading: An arena can join the fight
cards.text: Many stages return from Dead or Alive 3 and 4, while a new arena based on Metroid: Other M brings hazards associated with Team Ninja's work on that game. These surroundings matter because a useful attack can also change where the opponent lands. Arcade, Survival and training modes provide different ways to practise the same exchanges outside Chronicle. Dimensions makes its collection accessible through those repeated encounters: the history can be followed as a story, then revisited as a cast of fighters whose movements become more familiar through play.
